title: Minimum Cost to Make All Characters Equal
statement:
`s` is a binary string of length `n`, indexed from 0. You may use either of these operations as many times as you like, choosing any index `i` each time:

- flip every character of the prefix `s[0..i]`, which costs `i + 1`;
- flip every character of the suffix `s[i..n - 1]`, which costs `n - i`.

Flipping a character turns `'0'` into `'1'` and `'1'` into `'0'`. Return the smallest total cost that leaves every character of `s` the same, whether all `'0'` or all `'1'`.
notes:
## Intuition

Look at the boundaries between neighbours instead of the characters: the string is uniform exactly when no two neighbours differ. Flipping a prefix flips both characters of every pair inside it, so those pairs stay equal or unequal as before; only the pair straddling its right edge changes. A suffix flip likewise changes only the pair at its left edge. So every operation toggles exactly one boundary. The boundary between `i - 1` and `i` can be toggled by flipping `s[0..i-1]` (cost `i`) or `s[i..n-1]` (cost `n - i`), and boundaries never affect each other, so each differing boundary is fixed once at the cheaper price. A brute force would instead search all 2^n strings for the cheapest path, which only works for tiny inputs.

## Approach

1. Let `n` be the length of `s` and start `cost` at 0.
2. For each `i` from 1 to `n - 1`, compare `s[i]` with `s[i - 1]`.
3. If they differ, add `Math.min(i, n - i)`: the cheaper of flipping the `i` characters on the left or the `n - i` characters on the right.
4. Return `cost`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "0011"`, `n = 4`.

- `i = 1`: `'0'` and `'0'` match; nothing to pay.
- `i = 2`: `'1'` differs from `'0'`; add `min(2, 4 - 2) = 2`, so `cost = 2`.
- `i = 3`: `'1'` and `'1'` match.

The answer is `2` (flip the suffix `"11"`). For example 2, `"010101"`, every boundary differs and the costs are `1 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 9`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass over the neighbouring pairs.
- Space: O(1): only `cost` and the loop index.

## Pitfalls

- Fixing boundary `i` with a prefix flips `s[0..i-1]`, which costs `i`, not `i + 1`; the suffix costs `n - i`.
- There is no need to try "all `'0'`" and "all `'1'`" separately: removing every differing boundary reaches whichever is cheaper.
- Always flipping prefixes (or always suffixes) overpays for boundaries on the far side; pick the cheaper side per boundary.
- The total can reach about `n² / 4 ≈ 2.5 * 10^9`, beyond a 32-bit int, so use `long` in Java and `long long` in C.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `s` |
| `cost` | total paid so far |
| `i` | right-hand index of the boundary between `s[i - 1]` and `s[i]` |

narration.2: Remember the length; it sets the price of suffix flips.
narration.4: Visit every boundary, between positions i - 1 and i.
narration.5: Only a boundary where the neighbours differ needs an operation.
narration.6: Fix it with the cheaper flip: the i characters on the left or the n - i characters on the right.
narration.9: Every differing boundary has been paid for once; that is the minimum cost.
